title: Stock buy: Ategrity is industrializing E&S underwriting for SMBs
description: Ategrity Specialty focuses on excess-and-surplus insurance for small and mid-sized businesses — a tech-enabled underwriting platform with early public-market earnings momentum.
lede: Excess-and-surplus insurance is where standard markets say no. Ategrity’s bet is that the SMB slice of that market can be underwritten with production-line speed — and still underwrite a profit.
tldr: Ategrity Specialty Insurance Company Holdings (ASIC) is an E&S P&C insurer focused on small and medium-sized U.S. businesses.
Products span general liability, commercial property, management liability, and specialty professional lines distributed through brokerage channels.
Q1 2026 net income rose sharply year over year as the young public company scaled premium and underwriting profitability.
The thesis is tech-enabled “productionized” underwriting in a large, fragmented E&S SMB market.
Catastrophe loss, pricing competition, and reserving risk are the usual specialty insurance ways to lose money.
body_md:
## Business overview

**Ategrity Specialty (ASIC)** is a specialty property and casualty insurance holding company dedicated to the excess and surplus (E&S) market for SMBs across the United States. Underwriting runs through Ategrity Specialty Insurance Company, a Delaware-domiciled E&S insurer. The company went public in 2025 and still carries the footprint of a growth-stage specialty franchise rather than a diversified national carrier.

Product set includes general liability, commercial property, management liability, miscellaneous professional liability, allied healthcare, and architects & engineers coverage — sold into retail, real estate, hospitality, and construction end markets via brokers and small-business channels. The stated edge is not a unique line of business; it is process: data analytics, automation, and what management calls productionized underwriting for high volumes of smaller policies.

## Our buy thesis

We added Ategrity on June 18, 2026. We own ASIC because E&S for SMBs is structurally attractive and still fragmented. Admitted markets routinely decline or constrain risks that do not fit standard forms; surplus lines fill that gap at pricing that can be more responsive to risk. Serving that demand with low-touch, high-speed brokerage workflows is a real distribution advantage if loss ratios cooperate.

Early public financials have been encouraging. In Q1 2026, Ategrity reported net income attributable to stockholders of about $25.5 million ($0.51 per diluted share), up sharply from the prior-year period, with adjusted earnings essentially in line. That kind of step-change so soon after listing is why the name screens as a growth specialty rather than a sleepy mutual-style underwriter.

Valuation for a young E&S franchise embeds execution: keep growing gross written premium without drifting into poorly priced catastrophe or casualty pockets. We are underwriting that discipline — and the operating leverage of a digital-first expense base — not a one-quarter earnings pop.

## Growth and profitability

Growth comes from broker appointments, product expansion, and share gains in SMB E&S as the platform proves hit ratios and service levels. Profitability comes from combined ratio: loss ratio plus expense ratio. Automation should help the expense side; the loss side is always the open question in specialty insurance.

Investment income will matter more as surplus grows, but the core underwriting result is what we watch first. A specialty insurer that grows premium while the combined ratio stays comfortably below 100 can compound book value for years; the reverse destroys capital quickly.

## Valuation and momentum context

ASIC trades like a small-cap specialty insurer with growth expectations — often at a premium to slower mutual-conversion stories and at a discount to the largest E&S platforms. Momentum has followed earnings delivery and the post-IPO seasoning of the float. Liquidity is thinner than mega-cap financials; spreads and drawdowns can be sharp.

## Potential risks

- **Loss inflation and reserving.** Casualty lines can develop adversely years after the premium is earned.
- **Catastrophe and property aggregations.** Even SMB books can cluster geographically or by peril.
- **Pricing competition.** Softening E&S rates would pressure growth and margins simultaneously.
- **Reinsurance cost and availability.** Treaty pricing affects net risk retention and earnings volatility.
- **Scale and governance.** As a newer public company, operational and control risks remain higher than at multi-decade carriers.

## Concluding summary

Ategrity is a focused E&S franchise aiming to industrialize underwriting for the SMB segment that standard markets underserve. We hold ASIC for that niche, the early evidence of earnings power, and the long runway in specialty surplus lines — while treating every combined-ratio print as a fresh test of the thesis.
key_takeaway: ASIC is a bet on productionized E&S underwriting for SMBs — own it only as long as growth and underwriting margins move together.

title: Stock buy: Atlanticus is scaling inclusive credit with Mercury leverage
description: Atlanticus enables partners to offer consumer credit to Everyday Americans — and the Mercury acquisition is amplifying an already profitable Credit-as-a-Service platform.
lede: Most investors meet consumer credit through a bank brand. Atlanticus sits one layer underneath — the technology, analytics, and servicing engine that lets partners say yes to borrowers the prime system often ignores.
tldr: Atlanticus runs a Credit-as-a-Service platform spanning private-label retail and healthcare cards, general-purpose credit, and auto finance support.
Q1 2026 revenue roughly doubled year over year, with diluted EPS up ~50%, helped by Mercury Financial and 35% growth in legacy managed receivables.
The thesis is scale plus disciplined underwriting in a large under-served U.S. consumer segment — with acquisition integration as a near-term earnings lever.
Credit losses, funding markets, and fair-value loan accounting can swing results hard in either direction.
We hold ATLC as a specialty-finance compounder with tangible ROE and operating momentum.
body_md:
## Business overview

**Atlanticus Holdings (ATLC)** is a financial-technology company that helps bank, retail, healthcare, and automotive partners offer consumer credit to what management calls Everyday Americans — a large population that often sits outside traditional prime underwriting. Through its platform, Atlanticus supports private-label and general-purpose card products, healthcare financing, and auto-finance programs, drawing on decades of servicing experience and tens of billions in historical loan volume.

The economic model is not a simple lender-on-balance-sheet story. Atlanticus earns through a mix of interest and fee income on consumer receivables, partnership structures, and servicing economics, with a large book carried at fair value. That accounting can make quarter-to-quarter noise higher than a vanilla bank, but it also forces the market to mark credit reality more quickly.

The strategic event of the past year is the Mercury Financial acquisition. Two full quarters into ownership as of Q1 2026, management described integration as ahead of plan on portfolio actions, originations, unit economics, and operational combination into “one Atlanticus.”

## Our buy thesis

We added Atlanticus on April 17, 2026. We own it because inclusive credit is a structural market, not a fad — and because ATLC is one of the few scaled public platforms purpose-built for it. More than 100 million U.S. consumers sit in near-prime and non-prime segments that still need revolving and installment credit for retail, healthcare, and everyday spending. Banks periodically retreat from that risk; specialists who underwrite and service it well can earn attractive returns through the cycle.

Mercury is the accelerant, not the whole thesis. Legacy managed receivables grew about 35% excluding Mercury in Q1 — evidence the organic engine still works. Mercury adds receivables, distribution, and operating leverage if integration stays on track. Management reported net income attributable to common of $41.9 million, or $2.23 per diluted share, up roughly 50% year over year, with return on average equity near 27%.

That combination — organic growth, acquisitive scale, and high teens-to-twenties ROE — is rare in small-cap specialty finance. We would rather own a proven underwriting culture at a fair multiple than a prettier brand with untested credit boxes.

## Growth and profitability

Q1 total operating revenue was about $680 million, up 97% year over year, including roughly $224 million from Mercury. Net margin expanded more than 60% year over year to about $190 million. Those are acquisition-inflated growth rates, so we look through them to two cleaner signals: legacy receivables growth and whether Mercury unit economics are beating the deal model. On both counts, management’s commentary has been constructive.

Expense growth is real — you do not double a credit platform without people, data, and servicing cost — but it has lagged revenue growth enough to expand earnings. Cash generation was strong in the quarter, with hundreds of millions of operating cash flow and a sizable unrestricted cash balance against a leveraged funding stack typical for the industry.

Segment mix still skews heavily to Credit-as-a-Service versus Auto Finance. That concentration is fine while CaaS credit is behaving; it means vigilance on retail and card delinquency trends matters more than auto residual values for this name.

## Valuation and momentum context

Specialty finance often trades at a discount to fintech “platform” narratives even when ROE is superior, because investors correctly fear credit cycles. ATLC’s recent re-rating reflects earnings delivery and Mercury progress, not a free lunch. We are underwriting continued profitable growth and stable credit — if either slips, the multiple can compress quickly.

Relative to larger consumer lenders, Atlanticus remains a smaller, more opaque book. That opacity is why we write these notes: the edge is in reading partnership credit performance and funding access, not in a single headline PE.

## Potential risks

- **Credit cycle.** Non-prime and near-prime receivables are leveraged to employment and inflation in essentials.
- **Integration risk.** Mercury could still surprise on credit marks, retention, or cost to achieve “one Atlanticus.”
- **Funding markets.** Notes payable and securitization markets fund growth; a shut or expensive market slows originations.
- **Fair-value volatility.** Marks on loans at fair value can swing GAAP earnings independent of cash collections in the short run.
- **Regulatory and partner risk.** Bank partners, CARD Act-adjacent rules, and state lending regimes all shape product design.

## Concluding summary

Atlanticus is a scaled inclusive-credit platform with a newly enlarged receivable base, strong early Mercury integration signals, and ROE that specialty-finance investors should respect. We hold ATLC because Everyday Americans still need credit — and because this management team has shown it can grow that book profitably when peers pull back.
key_takeaway: Atlanticus earns its keep by underwriting the consumers banks underserve — Mercury is leverage on that franchise, not a replacement for credit discipline.

title: Stock buy: Roku’s streaming platform is finally printing real profits
description: Roku is the operating system of streaming for millions of households — and platform advertising plus subscriptions are now driving double-digit growth with expanding free cash flow.
lede: Roku spent a decade building the rails. The investment case today is simpler: those rails monetize through advertising and subscriptions, and the devices business is increasingly just the distribution tip of the spear.
tldr: Roku operates a leading TV streaming platform in the U.S., monetized primarily through platform advertising and subscriptions, with devices as a secondary line.
Q1 2026 platform revenue grew ~28% year over year; the company generated solid net income, adjusted EBITDA, and continued share repurchases.
The thesis is durable double-digit platform growth with margin expansion as ads and subscriptions scale on a largely fixed software base.
Ad cycles, competitive OS pressure (Google, Amazon, smart-TV OEMs), and content costs can interrupt the story.
We hold ROKU as a platform compounder exiting its “growth at all costs” era.
body_md:
## Business overview

**Roku (ROKU)** builds streaming players and, more importantly, the software platform that powers Roku OS on dedicated devices and licensed TVs. Users watch free ad-supported and paid streaming apps; Roku earns when advertisers buy audience, when consumers subscribe through the platform, and — to a lesser extent — when hardware ships.

Management now breaks Platform into Advertising and Subscriptions for clearer reporting. In Q1 2026, advertising and subscriptions were both material contributors inside $1.13 billion of platform revenue. The Roku Channel itself remains a major engagement surface — a first-party inventory pool that matters for ad yield.

Devices revenue is smaller and can be noisy (memory costs, promotions, unit mix). We treat hardware primarily as a customer-acquisition and retention tool for the higher-margin platform.

## Our buy thesis

We added Roku on May 15, 2026. We own it because streaming has won living rooms, and someone has to own the aggregation layer where apps, ads, and subscriptions meet. Roku’s installed base and hours streamed give it a scarce audience graph in a world where linear TV advertising keeps shrinking.

The financial transition is what made the stock ownable again for a fundamentals-first book. Q1 total net revenue was about $1.25 billion (+22% year over year), platform revenue +28%, with net income of $86 million and adjusted EBITDA of $148 million (+165% year over year). Free cash flow on a trailing basis hit new highs, and the company has been buying back stock under an authorized program — a shift from the years when dilution and losses dominated the narrative.

Full-year commentary has pointed to continued double-digit platform growth and further adjusted EBITDA margin expansion. We are underwriting that path: platform scale, mid-single-digit opex growth, and devices that do not need to be a profit center to justify the franchise.

## Growth and profitability

Advertising growth tracks streaming hours, ad load, and pricing (CPMs). Subscriptions growth tracks attach rates for The Roku Channel Premium and partner offers through the platform. Both benefit from engagement; Q1 streaming hours were still up year over year even as the category matures.

Platform gross margins in the low-to-mid 50s are the economic heart of the company. Incremental ad dollars and subscription revenue should continue to drop through at attractive rates if content and revenue-share costs stay disciplined. That is the operating leverage we care about — not unit sales of players.

## Valuation and momentum context

ROKU still carries a growth multiple, but it is increasingly an FCF and platform-growth debate rather than a faith-based TAM story. Estimate revisions have improved with profitability; that can reverse if ad budgets freeze. We prefer owning it while the company is still early in proving mid-teens-or-better platform growth can coexist with rising cash returns.

## Potential risks

- **Advertising recession.** Platform revenue is still ad-sensitive; a sharp cut in brand or performance spend hits fast.
- **Platform competition.** Google TV, Fire TV, and OEM smart-TV software fight for the same default home screen.
- **Content and revenue share.** Rising costs to secure apps or ad inventory can pressure platform margins.
- **Hardware margin noise.** Component costs (e.g., memory) can swing devices profitability and distract the market.
- **Engagement maturation.** Hours growth slowing structurally would cap ad and subscription upside.

## Concluding summary

Roku is the rare consumer-internet platform that already touches tens of millions of living rooms and is now converting that reach into advertising, subscriptions, and free cash flow. We hold ROKU for that monetization phase — with eyes open to ad-cycle and competitive risk.
key_takeaway: Underwrite Roku on platform advertising and subscriptions — treat devices as distribution, and respect how quickly ad cycles can change the tape.

title: Stock buy: Sezzle’s BNPL platform is compounding engagement and earnings
description: Sezzle is turning buy-now-pay-later into a subscription-led consumer platform — with rising purchase frequency, expanding product surface, and raised 2026 earnings guidance.
lede: Sezzle started as a point-of-sale installment product. What we own today is a consumer engagement engine — and the financials are finally catching up to that ambition.
tldr: Sezzle provides point-of-sale installment credit and a growing suite of subscription and wallet products in the U.S. and Canada.
Q1 2026 showed record purchase frequency and ~48% year-over-year growth in active subscribers, with management raising full-year adjusted EPS guidance.
The thesis is platform density: more products per user, higher frequency, and improving unit economics — not just gross merchandise volume.
Credit risk, funding costs, and regulatory scrutiny of BNPL remain the main ways the story can break.
We hold SEZL in the live book as a high-conviction fintech compounder with operating leverage still ahead of it.
body_md:
## Business overview

**Sezzle Inc. (SEZL)** is a payments and consumer-finance company built around buy-now-pay-later (BNPL). At checkout, eligible consumers can split a purchase into installments — typically pay-in-four over six weeks — while merchants get paid and Sezzle underwrites and funds the receivable. That core product still matters, but it is no longer the whole company.

Over the past few years Sezzle has layered subscription products (Premium, Anywhere), a virtual card that works beyond integrated merchants, stored-value balance features, longer-duration lending for qualified users, and — more recently — adjacent services like mobile plans inside the app. The strategic idea is familiar if you follow consumer fintech: turn a transactional payment tool into a daily financial relationship.

Geography is focused. Sezzle operates primarily in the United States and Canada and has been winding down smaller international footprints. That concentration matters for underwriting quality and regulatory clarity even if it caps the total addressable market relative to global BNPL peers.

## Our buy thesis

We added Sezzle to the live book on April 10, 2026. We own it because the company is proving that engagement can compound faster than pure GMV stories usually do. In Q1 2026, management highlighted a new high in average quarterly purchase frequency (about 7.1×) and active-subscriber growth of roughly 48% year over year. Those are not vanity metrics for a lender — they are the inputs to lower marketing drag, better credit selection, and more fee surface per user.

The second part of the thesis is product breadth. BNPL alone is a crowded, often capital-intensive category. A platform that can monetize subscriptions, on-demand access, longer-term credit, and adjacent services has more ways to earn on the same customer relationship. Sezzle’s recent launches — including mobile and expanded long-term lending — are early, but they fit the pattern of increasing wallet share rather than chasing one more merchant logo.

Third, the earnings trajectory has turned. After years of market skepticism that BNPL economics could work at scale, Sezzle raised 2026 guidance following Q1 — pointing to roughly 30–35% total revenue growth and about $5.10 of adjusted net income per diluted share. We care less about the precise print than about the direction: growth with rising profitability, not growth at any cost.

> **What we are not arguing**
>
> This is not a bet that BNPL replaces credit cards industry-wide. It is a bet that Sezzle can keep deepening a younger, digitally native cohort — and convert that engagement into durable earnings — while peers stay stuck in thinner, more promotional models.

## Growth and profitability

Top-line growth is still tied to how much consumers spend through Sezzle and how many of them pay for enhanced access. The encouraging shift is the mix: subscription and higher-frequency users create a more predictable revenue base than one-off checkout conversions. Record GMV in Q1 sat alongside that engagement flywheel, which is the combination we want to see.

On profitability, the operating story is leverage on underwriting, servicing, and technology. Management has emphasized in-house credit models and AI tooling for support and decisioning — the kind of cost structure that can expand margins if credit losses stay contained. Adjusted net income guidance stepping up through early 2026 is the market’s shorthand for that operating leverage arriving.

Funding remains central. Sezzle uses warehouse and credit facilities to finance receivables; cheaper, more durable funding supports both growth and margin. The company has continued to expand facility capacity as volumes grow — a positive if covenants and cost of funds remain manageable, a risk if credit markets tighten.

## Valuation and momentum context

SEZL has already re-rated hard as profitability became visible, so this is not a “cheap on trailing multiples” story in the classic value sense. We hold it because forward earnings power and engagement trends still look under-appreciated relative to the duration of the platform build-out — and because the live book can tolerate a higher-beta fintech when the fundamentals are accelerating.

Price momentum has been strong for a reason: estimate revisions and guidance raises followed real operating progress. That can reverse quickly if credit losses spike or growth decelerates. We size with that volatility in mind and treat the position as a thesis that needs ongoing confirmation each quarter.

## Potential risks

- **Credit deterioration.** BNPL and longer-duration consumer credit are cyclical. A weaker labor market or rising delinquencies would hit both provisions and growth appetite.
- **Funding and interest rates.** Higher funding costs compress net interest / fee economics even if volumes hold.
- **Regulation.** Consumer-credit rules, disclosure standards, and bank partnership structures can change the product set overnight.
- **Competition.** Affirm, PayPal, Apple, shop-pay installments, and bank cards all fight for the same checkout moment.
- **Execution on adjacent products.** Mobile plans and new lending products can distract or add risk if they do not clear the same unit-economic bar as the core platform.

## Concluding summary

Sezzle is no longer just a BNPL ticker. It is a consumer platform with rising frequency, expanding subscriptions, and a management team willing to raise earnings guidance as those trends show up in the numbers. We own it for that compounding loop — engagement supporting credit quality and monetization — while staying honest about how fast consumer-credit stories can unwind.
key_takeaway: Own Sezzle for platform engagement and rising earnings power — not as a simple GMV growth trade. Confirm credit, funding, and subscriber trends every quarter.

title: Stock buy: Skyward Specialty is building a broader specialty P&C platform
description: Skyward Specialty underwrites niche commercial risks in the U.S. and, via Apollo, at Lloyd’s — a specialty insurer diversifying premium and fee income after a transformative acquisition.
lede: Specialty insurance rewards underwriters who know a niche better than the market. Skyward’s evolution is about collecting more of those niches — including a Lloyd’s platform — without losing the underwriting plot.
tldr: Skyward Specialty (SKWD) is a specialty P&C insurer serving commercial customers in niche and hard-to-place risks.
Beginning in 2026, results report Skyward Specialty and Apollo (Lloyd’s) segments separately, reflecting a broader platform.
Q1 2026 net earned premiums rose to ~$434M from ~$300M a year earlier, with underwriting fee income appearing via Apollo.
The thesis is diversified specialty premium growth plus fee income, with underwriting margin as the gatekeeper.
Acquisition integration, loss inflation, and reinsurance markets are the main risks.
body_md:
## Business overview

**Skyward Specialty Insurance Group (SKWD)** underwrites specialty commercial property and casualty risks — the kinds of accounts that need tailored forms, higher expertise, or surplus-lines flexibility. Distribution is brokerage-driven, and the culture is closer to a collection of underwriting boxes than a personal-auto assembly line.

The Apollo acquisition expanded Skyward into Lloyd’s platform operations, including managed syndicates and managing-agency activities. From Q1 2026, the company reports a Skyward Specialty segment (U.S. brand) and an Apollo segment, plus corporate. That structure matters: investors can now see U.S. underwriting separately from Lloyd’s underwriting and fee income.

## Our buy thesis

We added Skyward on July 2, 2026. We own it because specialty commercial insurance remains one of the better places in P&C to earn underwriting profit when leadership stays disciplined. Niche books can reprice faster than mass-market personal lines, and skilled underwriters can walk away from stupid risk — a cultural advantage that shows up in combined ratios over time.

Apollo adds geographic and product diversification plus underwriting fee income ($10.1 million in Q1 2026) that does not rely solely on taking insurance risk. Net earned premiums of $434 million in Q1 (versus $300 million a year earlier) show the scale step-up. Gross written premium across both segments exceeded $660 million in the quarter.

Near term, the stock is an execution story: prove that the combined platform can grow profitably without adverse development or cultural dilution. Medium term, it is a compounding specialty franchise with more levers than the pre-deal Skyward alone.

## Growth and profitability

Growth drivers include rate, exposure, new programs, and Apollo contribution. Profitability hinges on accident-year loss ratios, prior-year reserve development, expense discipline, and reinsurance spend. Net investment income also rose year over year in Q1 as the balance sheet grew — a helpful but secondary earnings stream.

We care most about whether Skyward Specialty’s U.S. book still underwrites to an attractive ex-Apollo combined ratio while Apollo’s returns (underwriting plus fees) clear the cost of capital. Segment reporting makes that monitoring easier than it was at deal close.

## Valuation and momentum context

SKWD typically trades as a small/mid-cap specialty insurer — sensitive to combined ratio prints and M&A skepticism. The shares can look expensive on trailing earnings after a strong specialty cycle and cheap if you believe the Apollo platform earns through a softer market. Our stance is process over price: hold while underwriting metrics cooperate; reassess quickly if they do not.

## Potential risks

- **Reserve development.** Specialty casualty can surprise years later.
- **Integration risk.** Lloyd’s platforms have cultural and operational complexity.
- **Catastrophe and clash risk.** Property and specialty aggregations can produce outsized losses.
- **Reinsurance pricing.** Harder reinsurance markets raise net volatility or push rate needs higher.
- **Competition.** Other specialty and E&S writers can chase the same niches when capital is abundant.

## Concluding summary

Skyward Specialty is a niche commercial insurer that has widened its aperture through Apollo without abandoning the specialty playbook. We hold SKWD for underwriting-led compounding across U.S. and Lloyd’s platforms — measured always by the combined ratio, not the press release.
key_takeaway: Specialty insurance only works with underwriting discipline — Apollo diversifies Skyward, but the combined ratio still decides the thesis.

title: Stock buy: SoFi’s everything-app is delivering growth and real earnings
description: SoFi is compounding members, products, and fee income across lending, deposits, and brokerage — with Q1 2026 showing record revenue and sustained profitability.
lede: SoFi’s pitch was always ambitious: one app for borrowing, saving, spending, investing, and advice. The question for years was whether that bundle could earn. The live numbers say it can.
tldr: SoFi is a member-centric digital financial services platform with lending, deposits, brokerage, and technology (Galileo) businesses.
Q1 2026 delivered record adjusted net revenue of ~$1.1B (+41% YoY), net income of $167M, and continued member growth toward a 14.7M base.
The thesis is diversified fee and net-interest income on a growing member base — with bank charter advantages funding loans more cheaply than non-bank lenders.
Credit losses, deposit competition, and capital markets for loan sales remain key risks.
We hold SOFI as a scaled digital-bank compounder with Rule-of-40 style growth.
body_md:
## Business overview

**SoFi Technologies (SOFI)** operates an “everything app” for digital financial services: personal loans, student-loan products, credit cards, deposits, investing, and financial advice, plus Galileo, a technology platform that powers accounts for other fintechs and brands. Members can originate multiple products inside one relationship — the cross-sell motion that traditional banks talk about and rarely execute digitally.

As a bank holding company, SoFi funds a large share of lending with deposits, which is structurally different from marketplace lenders that rely entirely on whole-loan sales or warehouse lines. That does not eliminate credit risk; it changes the funding stack and the path to net interest margin.

## Our buy thesis

We added SoFi on June 5, 2026. We own it because member growth and product intensity are showing up as both revenue and profit. Q1 adjusted net revenue of about $1.1 billion was up 41% year over year; adjusted EBITDA rose ~62%; GAAP net income was $167 million. Management highlighted an 18th consecutive quarter above a Rule-of-40 threshold — shorthand for combining growth and margin in a way growth-stage fintechs often fail to do.

Loan originations remain a primary engine (record quarterly originations in Q1), but the longer-duration story is fee diversification: brokerage, referrals, interchange, and Galileo. A member who holds deposits and invests with SoFi is stickier and more valuable than a one-time personal-loan borrower.

Full-year 2026 guidance has pointed to roughly 30% adjusted net revenue growth, mid-30s EBITDA margins, and mid-teens net income margins. We treat guidance as a map, not a promise — but the map is consistent with the multi-year shift from “story stock” to operating company.

## Growth and profitability

Growth comes from new members (management targeting at least ~30% member growth in 2026), more products per member, and healthy origination volumes without reckless credit boxes. Profitability comes from deposit-funded NIM, fee attach, and operating leverage on technology and marketing as the brand scales.

Credit is the swing factor. Personal loans and cards will produce losses; the question is whether risk-adjusted returns clear the cost of capital through the cycle. SoFi’s recent results suggest underwriting and pricing have been ahead of losses — a condition we re-check every quarter rather than assume permanently.

## Valuation and momentum context

SOFI often trades between fintech narrative multiples and bank multiples, which creates volatility whenever the market re-labels the story. Momentum has followed earnings beats and member metrics; that can unwind on a credit headline. We own it for the operating trajectory, not for a clean “cheap bank” screen.

## Potential risks

- **Credit cycle.** Consumer loan losses can rise faster than revenue if unemployment turns or underwriting drifts.
- **Deposit competition.** Higher deposit betas compress NIM when rates or competitive offers move against SoFi.
- **Capital markets.** Loan sales and securitizations still matter for balance-sheet management; a shut market forces awkward choices.
- **Regulatory oversight.** Bank supervision, consumer-lending rules, and capital requirements constrain growth levers.
- **Competition.** Incumbent banks, other neobanks, and big-tech wallets all chase the same member.

## Concluding summary

SoFi is turning a crowded digital-banking narrative into a diversified earnings stream: lending at scale, deposits as funding, and fee businesses on top. We hold SOFI because the member flywheel is visible in the financials — and because profitable growth in consumer finance is rarer than slide decks suggest.
key_takeaway: SoFi works when members, products, and risk-adjusted lending returns move together — watch credit and deposit costs as closely as the growth headlines.

title: Stock buy: Western Digital is the AI era’s mass-capacity storage pick
description: Post-split Western Digital is a pure-play HDD franchise riding hyperscale AI data growth — with record margins, long-term customer agreements, and a repaired balance sheet.
lede: Hard disk drives were supposed to be a sunset industry. Then AI data centers remembered that the cheapest place to park an exabyte is still spinning rust — and Western Digital became interesting again.
tldr: Western Digital (WDC), after separating flash, is a focused mass-capacity HDD supplier to cloud and enterprise customers.
Fiscal Q3 2026 revenue rose ~45% year over year with record ~50.5% gross margin and a swing to net cash.
The thesis is secular exabyte demand from AI (especially inference and data retention) inside a disciplined HDD duopoly with Seagate.
Technology roadmap risk (HAMR vs competing approaches), customer concentration, and cyclical CapEx pauses are the main threats.
We hold WDC as an AI-infrastructure compounder with real free-cash-flow yield — not as a nostalgia hardware trade.
body_md:
## Business overview

**Western Digital (WDC)** designs and sells high-capacity hard disk drives used primarily in cloud data centers for nearline and archival storage. After the separation of its flash business, the equity story is cleaner: one franchise, one set of customers, one technology roadmap around areal density (ePMR, UltraSMR, HAMR) and cost per terabyte.

Cloud already represents the vast majority of revenue — on the order of ~90% in recent quarters — which means hyperscaler demand, pricing, and long-term agreements dominate the outlook. Consumer and OEM channels matter less than they did in the PC-centric era.

## Our buy thesis

We added Western Digital on July 17, 2026. We own it because AI creates data faster than flash economics can store it at scale. Training runs, checkpoints, inference logs, and retention policies push exabytes into cold and warm tiers where HDDs remain several times cheaper per TB than enterprise SSD. That is not a 2012 “PC refresh” cycle; it is a structural storage workload.

The industry structure helps. Mass-capacity HDD is effectively a duopoly with Seagate (plus a smaller third player). When both leaders stay disciplined on capacity, pricing power returns. WDC has talked about long-term agreements extending into the late decade and about sold-out or tightly allocated supply — the opposite of the inventory gluts that wrecked prior cycles.

Fiscal Q3 2026 illustrated the earnings torque: roughly $3.3 billion of revenue (+45% year over year), gross margin above 50%, nearly doubled EPS, nearly $1 billion of free cash flow in the quarter, debt reduction into a net cash position, and a higher dividend. Management also lifted conviction on long-term exabyte growth to something like a mid-20% CAGR. Those are the fundamentals of a re-rated industrial, not a dying disk maker.

## Growth and profitability

Growth is exabyte shipments times price per TB, improved by mix toward higher-capacity drives (40TB-class ePMR, HAMR ramps, UltraSMR adoption). Profitability has expanded because mix, pricing, and utilization moved together. Sustaining 50%+ gross margins is not guaranteed — it is the bull case we monitor, not a law of physics.

Technology execution is the quiet battleground. Seagate has been aggressive on HAMR commercialization; WDC has leaned on advanced ePMR/UltraSMR while qualifying its own HAMR products with hyperscalers. Either company can win share with a better cost-per-TB curve. We own WDC for the sector thesis and current margin reality, while watching relative roadmap progress each quarter.

## Valuation and momentum context

WDC has already rerated with the AI-storage narrative and the balance-sheet clean-up. The debate is duration: how many years of tight supply and AI data growth the market will pay for. Momentum is strong; cyclical hardware can give it back quickly if hyperscalers pause. We size accordingly and focus on FCF and margin resilience over peak multiple arguments.

## Potential risks

- **Hyperscaler CapEx air pocket.** Even if data is cumulative, purchase timing is lumpy.
- **Technology share shift.** A competitor cost curve that undercuts WDC would pressure price and mix.
- **Customer concentration.** A handful of cloud buyers dominate demand.
- **Margin mean reversion.** 50%+ gross margins invite competition and customer pushback over time.
- **Macro and export / supply-chain shocks.** Manufacturing and component constraints can interrupt shipments.

## Concluding summary

Western Digital is a pure-play bet that AI’s data exhaust needs mass-capacity HDD, delivered by a disciplined duopoly with pricing power and a repaired balance sheet. We hold WDC for that secular storage demand — and we will keep testing whether margins and roadmap execution justify the re-rating.
key_takeaway: WDC works as an AI data-storage compounder inside an HDD duopoly — underwrite exabyte growth and margin durability, not a permanent 50% gross-margin regime.

title: Stock buy: WisdomTree is compounding AUM across ETFs, privates, and digital
description: WisdomTree is an asset manager with record AUM, a higher fee mix, and optionality in tokenized assets and private markets — a scaled compounder in a consolidating industry.
lede: Asset managers usually die by fee compression. WisdomTree’s pitch is the opposite: grow AUM in differentiated products — and keep enough pricing power that revenue outruns the industry’s race to zero.
tldr: WisdomTree manages a global suite of ETPs, models, digital-asset products, and — via Ceres — U.S. farmland / private-market exposure.
Q1 2026 ending AUM hit a record ~$152.6B; operating revenue rose ~47% year over year on higher AUM, fees, and Ceres contribution.
The thesis is diversified AUM growth plus innovation in tokenization and private markets, not a pure beta bet on equities.
Market drawdowns, crypto volatility, and fee wars remain the primary risks.
We hold WT as a capital-light compounder with multiple growth engines.
body_md:
## Business overview

**WisdomTree (WT)** is a global asset manager best known for exchange-traded products, with an expanding footprint in digital assets (including tokenized real-world assets and related infrastructure such as WisdomTree Prime and Connect) and private markets following the Ceres Partners farmland platform acquisition. Clients span advisors, institutions, and increasingly direct digital channels.

Economics are classic asset management: advisory fees on AUM, plus other product and platform revenues. Operating leverage is high when markets cooperate and net flows are positive; the inverse is also true. WisdomTree’s differentiation is product mix — thematic, currency-hedged, commodity, crypto-related, and private-market sleeves — rather than being the cheapest S&P 500 clone.

## Our buy thesis

We added WisdomTree on May 1, 2026. We own it because AUM scale finally looks like a flywheel instead of a perpetual turnaround story. Record ending AUM near $153 billion in Q1 2026, up both sequentially and year over year, came from a mix of net inflows and market appreciation. Average AUM and a higher average advisory fee helped operating revenue jump sharply versus the prior year.

The second leg is strategic positioning. Tokenization and on-chain distribution are still early, but WisdomTree has spent years building regulatory and product infrastructure while larger managers waited. Private markets via Ceres add a stickier, less index-correlated AUM pool. Neither needs to “win the internet” for the core ETF franchise to keep compounding; they are call options attached to a real cash-generative business.

Third, the industry backdrop favors scaled specialists. Advisors continue to migrate from mutual funds to ETFs, and clients want differentiated exposures — gold, income, crypto beta, alternatives — without leaving a familiar wrapper. WisdomTree already lives in those categories.

## Growth and profitability

Growth drivers are net flows, market levels, and fee mix. Q1 showed all three helping at once: higher average AUM, a richer advisory fee, European ETP other revenue, and Ceres contribution. That is an unusually clean setup; we do not assume it repeats every quarter.

Profitability in asset management is mostly about keeping compensation and distribution costs from eating fee gains. When AUM gaps higher, incremental margins can be excellent. When risk assets sell off or crypto products go out of favor, revenue falls faster than management can cut. That operating leverage is why we size WT as a compounder with cycle risk, not as ballast.

## Valuation and momentum context

WT tends to trade as a small/mid-cap asset manager — sensitive to flows headlines and equity beta — rather than as a pure fintech multiple. The stock has benefited from AUM records and product momentum; valuation embeds continued execution on flows and digital initiatives. We are underwriting durable mid-teens-or-better growth in earnings power through the cycle, not a one-quarter fee spike.

## Potential risks

- **Market beta.** A broad risk-off tape shrinks AUM and fee revenue regardless of product quality.
- **Fee compression.** Competitors can reprice overlapping exposures and pressure advisory fees.
- **Crypto and digital-asset volatility.** Related AUM and sentiment can swing violently.
- **Integration and execution.** Ceres and new digital products must clear return hurdles after deal and build costs.
- **Regulatory change.** ETF, crypto, and alternative-product rules evolve continuously across jurisdictions.

## Concluding summary

WisdomTree is a scaled ETP franchise with record AUM, improving fee mix, and credible optionality in digital assets and private markets. We hold WT because capital-light fee businesses that still grow are scarce — and because this one is no longer defined only by the last cycle’s skepticism.
key_takeaway: WisdomTree compounds when differentiated AUM grows faster than fee pressure — watch flows, fee mix, and whether digital/private initiatives stay additive.
